newsitem.title: USA: Mexican growth to simmer, not boil -- Fleming.
newsitem.headline: Mexican growth to simmer, not boil -- Fleming.

text.p: Mexico's economic recovery has brought a surge of investment in Mexican equities, but an expected slowdown in exports and business inventories could dampen the festive mood, said Omar Borla, chief economist at Robert Fleming Inc, in a research report.

A pick-up in growth during the third quarter, decreasing unemployment and attractive stock prices were just a few of the elements that lured new investment into Mexico's stock market over the past few months, Borla said.
But Borla questioned how rapid an economic expansion Mexico can sustain.
Exports have been one of the driving forces behind Mexico's economic growth, Borla said. But exports are expanding at a decreasing rate, he noted.

"The size of the economy, population, and the low value-added characteristic of its manufacturing sector almost make it impossible for Mexico to continue expanding exports at a high rate," Borla said in the report.

Borla said Mexico exhibits the stages of an "exports recovery model" rather than an "exports growth model." Under to this model, exports expand strongly during a recession but turn sluggish as soon as an economic recovery begins.

Exports "can help pull the economy out from the recession, as producers can redirect their products from domestic to international markets," Borla said. This should trigger stronger economic expansion during an economic expansion but slow down as the first sign of an economic recovery of the domestic market is apparent, the Fleming report said.

So the small trade surplus achieved since the December 1994 devaluation has almost disappeard, while the maquiladoras -- foreign plants using Mexican workers -- maintain an almost constant export surplus over their intermediate goods imports, it said.
"This relationship is also a clear example of the low value-added characteristic of the manufacturing sector," the report said.
Another limiting factor of Mexican economic growth is inventory buildup, according to Borla.

Manufacturers began an inventory-reduction program after the December 1994 devaluation, when inflation and interest rates shot up. The process reversed in the second quarter of 1996 after improvements in demand, inflation and rates, Borla said.

But "a continued expansion of inventory is out of the question," Borla said. Expectations of stronger demand improvements will fall short of reality, prompting producers to keep inventories in check, he said.
Evidence of declining demand will show up in the Retail Sale Index, which usually spikes in December as consumers spend yearend bonuses, Borla said.
Wage increases consistent with or slightly below inflation, however, will limit the spike this year, he said.
Furthermore, aggregate income is growing more slowly as the workforce becomes more heavily made up of unskilled workers, Borla said.
